title: WOOLHEAD v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In Woolhead v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Woolhead, is a British citizen of Romany Gypsy origin, falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. He brought a case against the United Kingdom after being refused planning permission to live in a caravan with his family on his own land in North Weald, Essex. The harm at the centre of the case concerned the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller individuals who, due to planning restrictions and a shortage of authorised sites, face obstacles in maintaining their traditional way of life and risk being forced into illegality or homelessness.

Mr. Woolhead, who had lived a nomadic lifestyle since childhood, purchased land in 1984 and settled there with his family. Despite the site’s previous use for vehicle repairs, local authorities issued enforcement notices and repeatedly refused planning permission for his caravan, citing green belt policies. Although a planning inspector recognised special circumstances and recommended approval, the Secretary of State ultimately dismissed the appeal in 1992, arguing that no exceptional justification existed for development in the green belt and that alternative sites might be available.

The European Commission of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 (right to respect for home and private life), Article 6 (fair trial), Article 14 (non-discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (property). However, it declared the application inadmissible, finding that the authorities’ actions fell within their margin of appreciation and that procedural safeguards had been respected.

This case highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing lawful accommodation and recognition of their cultural identity, reflecting broader patterns of exclusion in the late twentieth century.
